segments.title: HMS Rutherford’s American-built origin
segments.summary: HMS Rutherford was a Captain-class frigate built in the United States as a Buckley-class destroyer escort and employed by the Royal Navy from 1943 to 1945.
segments.body: Rutherford was K558, an American-built escort that served in the Royal Navy as a Captain-class frigate. The United States had built her as a Buckley-class destroyer escort, so her American and British classifications refer to the same ship. Her Royal Navy service lasted from 1943 to 1945. The introduction places her coastal-forces command work in the final years of the Second World War.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies K558 as a Captain-class frigate built as a Buckley-class destroyer escort and gives her Royal Navy service dates.

segments.title: An escort designed for reach rather than speed
segments.summary: Rutherford’s dimensions, boiler plant, 24-knot top speed, and 5,500-nautical-mile range explain why endurance mattered more than high speed for this escort.
segments.body: Rutherford displaced roughly 1,400 tons and measured about 93 metres long and 11 metres across, with a draught of 2.5 to 2.7 metres. Two Foster Wheeler express D-type water-tube boilers produced about 13,500 shaft horsepower, enough for a top speed of roughly 24 knots. That was sufficient for her role even though it was not especially fast. At 15 knots she could cover about 5,500 nautical miles, pairing modest speed with the range needed for escort work.

evidence.note: The transcript lists the frigate’s displacement, dimensions, boiler plant, speed, and endurance.

segments.title: Anti-aircraft and anti-submarine weapons for coastal work
segments.summary: Rutherford carried three 3-inch guns, a twin 40 mm Bofors mounting, up to sixteen 20 mm Oerlikons, Hedgehog, and depth charges.
segments.body: Rutherford carried three 3-inch guns and one twin 40 mm Bofors mounting. Her 20 mm Oerlikon battery ranged from seven to sixteen guns at different points in her career, with the number increasing as D-Day approached. A Mark 10 Hedgehog anti-submarine mortar and depth charges gave her weapons for attacking submerged targets. The resulting armament combined close-range gun defence with dedicated anti-submarine weapons on a coastal-forces command frigate.

evidence.note: The transcript lists the gun armament, the enlarged 20 mm battery near D-Day, Hedgehog, and depth charges.

segments.title: A radar-equipped command ship for motor torpedo boats
segments.summary: SA and SL radar, Type 144 ASDIC, and direction-finding equipment made Rutherford an information hub for smaller motor torpedo boats.
segments.body: Rutherford's SA and SL radar sets, Type 144 ASDIC, and medium- and high-frequency direction-finding antennas gave her the sensor fit needed for command work. A command ship gathered information and passed it to smaller motor torpedo boats that could not carry the same equipment. This made the frigate an information and coordination centre for a coastal-forces flotilla. Destroyers sometimes took over because they carried the same equipment and more, and a destroyer flotilla leader could fill the command role on particular operations. Her value as a command ship lay in sensors and information flow rather than firepower alone.

evidence.note: The transcript lists Rutherford’s sensors and explains her information-sharing command role alongside motor torpedo boats and occasional destroyer flotilla leaders.
